title: Boredom with routine
hook: routine gets stale; change the form, keep the heart: the Hasidic tale of the whistling boy, and keva and kavanah
tomorrow: a son rehearsed a speech for the walk home. why didn't he finish it?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: doubt belongs. Thomas doubted out loud and stayed in the room. Today's break is quieter than doubt. It's a yawn.

Same route to work, same three apps every morning, the same words at the same hour until you're saying them on autopilot. Now a Hasidic tale. It's Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, and the synagogue is deep in the long prayers. A village boy stands at the back. He can't read the prayer book. He feels the prayers rising all around him, and he has one thing in his pocket: a little whistle. He puts it to his lips and blows. Heads turn. People are horrified.
screen: `THE SAME WORDS ON AUTOPILOT.` → `YOM KIPPUR, THE LONG PRAYERS.` → `A BOY WHO CAN'T READ.` → `HE BLOWS THE WHISTLE.`

segments.voice: Then, the tale says, the Baal Shem Tov, the teacher Hasidic tradition looks back to as its founder, stopped them. That whistle, he said, carried all our prayers up with it. The boy had the thing the routine was missing: kavanah, the heart turned toward God. The tale grows from an old Jewish argument. In the Mishnah, Rabbi Eliezer warns that whoever makes his prayer a fixed task, his prayer is not a plea. And the Talmud asks what fixed means. One answer: someone who can't add anything new to it. The words of Jewish prayer stayed set. The set prayers are still said, at set times. But that Talmud answer asks for something fresh inside them: a new thought, a new person to pray for. That's the Jewish teaching of keva and kavanah: the fixed form, and the heart inside it. Both are needed. Keva without kavanah goes stale. Kavanah without keva drifts. So when routine goes flat, the answer isn't to throw out the whole form. It's to change one small part, so the heart wakes up inside it.
screen: `THE WHISTLE CARRIED THE PRAYERS.` · `A FIXED TASK IS NOT A PLEA.` · `ADD SOMETHING NEW EACH DAY.` · `KEVA AND KAVANAH: FORM AND HEART.` · then, large: `FRESH FORM.`

segments.voice: Do today's sit from a different seat or posture than usual: by a window, standing, or facing the other way. Notice one thing you can only see from there. Same heart, fresh form, until the bell.
Boredom with routine: when the practice runs on autopilot, met by changing one part of the form so the heart wakes up, keva with kavanah.
Your line: fresh form. The boy's whistle was new; the prayer under it was not. Day 1674, and see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews pray set prayers at set times (keva) and are taught to bring intention (kavanah) to them, sometimes adding a personal request or a new melody. Hasidic tales like the whistling boy are told to stress the heart in prayer.
